kurz: How the number of people working, their wage per hour and their output per hour determine whether prosperity is created or merely redistributed.

bloecke.md:
The labour market is where overall economic developments turn into household income. All the purchasing power that an economy distributes arises from three quantities: the hours worked, the wage per hour and the amount produced in that hour. The first two fluctuate with the business cycle; the third determines developments over decades.

Labour market data, however, almost always appear as a rate. A rate is a fraction, and it also falls when unemployed people give up looking, so that the numerator and the denominator shrink by the same number.

## Definitions of unemployment

In Germany, the Federal Employment Agency counts people as unemployed under Section 16 SGB III (Social Code Book III, employment promotion) if they are registered with it, not in employment and available, and are themselves looking for work (Section 138 SGB III). People who work fewer than fifteen hours a week still count as not in employment in the statistics. Participants in active labour market policy measures, by contrast, do not count as unemployed under Section 16(2) SGB III. This is why the agency also publishes a figure for [[Underemployment (Unterbeschäftigung)|underemployment (Unterbeschäftigung)]], which adds these cases back in.

Eurostat and the US Bureau of Labor Statistics count differently. Under the ILO labour force concept, people count as employed if they worked for pay for at least one hour in the reference week. Only people who have actively looked for work and are available at short notice count as unemployed. Registration with an authority is not required. The ILO rate for Germany is therefore regularly well below the Federal Employment Agency's rate. There are thus two figures for the same country, based on two definitions.

bloecke.titel: Unemployment and inflation, as of August 2026
bloecke.unter: The German rate counts registered unemployed people and is not directly comparable with the other two, which follow the ILO concept. The headline rates differ, while the core rates in the third series are the same (all values August 2026).

bloecke.md: The first two groups of bars match the textbook picture in which more unemployment goes hand in hand with less inflation. The third group contradicts this impression. All three economies have a core rate of 2.4%, so the difference in the headline rates is due to energy prices, not to the labour market. In the US, the core rate is thus a full percentage point below the headline rate. An overheated labour market would produce the opposite relationship.

## Falling labour force participation

The US labour force participation rate stood at 61.6% in August 2026, 0.5 percentage points lower than in January. An unemployment rate of 4.1% with around 7.0 million unemployed people implies a labour force of about 171 million. This gives a reference population aged 16 and over of around 277 million.

If labour force participation had stayed constant at 62.1% since January 2026, the labour force would be around 172.1 million instead of 170.7 million, about 1.4 million more.

If these 1.4 million had been counted as unemployed, the rate would be 8.4 million / 172.1 million = 4.9% instead of 4.1%.

This is the upper limit of the effect, because people who leave the labour force often retire or go into education and would not look for work even if conditions were better. This does not change the direction. Falling participation makes the rate look more favourable.

The unemployment rate cannot be interpreted on its own. Only together with labour force participation and absolute employment does it show whether just the numerator or the denominator as well has become smaller.

## Job creation and labour supply

According to the first release, 162,000 nonfarm jobs were created in the US in August 2026 (133,000 after the revision of 2 October), significantly more than the twelve-month average of 31,000. The rate stayed at 4.1% even though hardly any jobs were created on average. The arithmetical reason is that labour supply grew just as slowly. The number of jobs an economy needs to keep the rate stable equals the growth in its labour force and is therefore not a fixed number. If supply falls, a few thousand jobs a month are enough.

Further data complete the picture. Weekly initial claims for unemployment benefits were 196,000 in mid-September 2026, after 204,000 to 207,000 in the previous weeks, and thus historically low. At the same time, the employment sub-index of the US services PMI stood at 47.8 points in August, indicating shrinking employment, while the overall index, at 55.4 points, clearly pointed to growth. So there are hardly any layoffs and hardly any new hires. The labour market is not collapsing, but it is barely moving. For employees, this means a low risk of dismissal and, at the same time, little bargaining power.

bloecke.md:
## Nominal wages and real wages

Average hourly earnings in the US rose by 3.1% year on year to $37.75 in August 2026. Consumer prices rose by 3.4% in the same month. The exact calculation gives 1.031 / 1.034 − 1 = −0.29%. The purchasing power of hourly earnings has therefore fallen slightly despite the pay rise. The simple subtraction (3.1 − 3.4 = −0.3) is a good approximation for small rates, but becomes noticeably inaccurate for double-digit rates.

For the euro area, the ECB reports moderate wage growth for 2026 combined with rising labour productivity. This combination dampens the rise in [[Unit labour costs|unit labour costs]]. It is through unit labour costs that the labour market affects the price level; the wage alone is not an adequate yardstick for this.

bloecke.formel: Unit labour cost growth ≈ Nominal wage growth − Productivity growth
bloecke.erklaerung: Unit labour costs are the labour costs per unit produced. If wages rise exactly as fast as productivity, unit labour costs remain constant. The pay rises then create no price pressure, and the entire increase reaches employees as a real wage gain. With an inflation target of 2%, wage growth equal to productivity growth plus 2 percentage points is therefore compatible with the target.
variablen: change in labour costs per hour
change in value added per hour worked
labour costs per unit of output, the variable that matters for prices
bloecke.beispiel: Wage growth of 4.0% with productivity growth of 1.5% results in a 2.5% rise in unit labour costs. With a constant profit margin, this corresponds to price growth of around 2.5% in the medium term, half a percentage point above the target.

bloecke.titel: Wage growth, productivity and the 2% target
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation of the rise in unit labour costs as a percentage. The cells showing 2.0 are compatible with the inflation target. The same collective wage agreement can be consistent with the target or inflationary, depending on productivity.

bloecke.md:
## Productivity and real wages

Productivity is the only lasting source of rising real wages; everything else is redistribution. Higher wages without higher productivity shift income from profits to wages, which is possible only to a limited extent and cannot be repeated. More working hours increase output, but not prosperity per hour of lifetime. Only if more is produced in the same hour can the real wage rise permanently without someone else getting less. The effect works slowly, but over decades it is powerful.

bloecke.titel: One percentage point more productivity growth over forty years
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with an index of 100 in the starting year. With growth of 1% a year, the index stands at 148.9 after forty years, with 2% at 220.8. Over the same period, this gives around two and a half times the increase.

bloecke.md: When an economy shifts from industry to services, measured productivity falls without anyone working less well. In care work or teaching, a working hour can hardly be intensified. Statistics capture only incompletely the quality gains in digital goods whose price is falling or zero. In addition, productivity per person can fall while productivity per hour rises, namely when weekly working hours fall. In any dispute about productivity, it should therefore first be clarified which of the two measures is meant.

## The Phillips curve and its limits

In 1958, A. W. Phillips used British data from 1861 to 1957 to show a negative relationship between unemployment and wage growth. In the 1960s, this gave rise to the political notion that a little more inflation could be traded for a little less unemployment. Friedman and Phelps objected at the end of the 1960s. They argued that employees expect inflation and build it into their wage demands. The trade-off would therefore only work as long as inflation came as a surprise. The 1970s, with high unemployment and high inflation at the same time, confirmed this view.

What remained was the expectations-augmented version. According to it, inflation depends on inflation expectations, on supply shocks and on the gap between unemployment and an inflation-stable rate, the [[NAIRU]]. This rate cannot be observed; it is estimated. Depending on the method and the decade, the estimates vary by several percentage points. Because its uncertainty band is wider than the fluctuation in unemployment over a business cycle, it is of no use for steering policy.

In the 2010s, the curve was empirically so flat that falling unemployment generated hardly any inflation. In 2021 and 2022, by contrast, it suddenly appeared steep. Both can be explained after the fact; neither could be exploited beforehand. In August 2026, the core rates were at 2.4% and the headline rates above that, while unemployment rates were moving sideways. The cause of the price increases therefore lies in energy prices, not in wages.

Central banks nevertheless keep an eye on wages. A supply shock raises the price level once. It only turns into lasting inflation through second-round effects. In these, employees demand compensation for lost purchasing power, companies pass on the higher costs, and the next round begins. The wage round decides whether a shock turns into a spiral.

In 2026, the data argue against such a spiral. Wages are growing moderately, productivity is rising, unit labour costs are subdued, and long-term inflation expectations are around 2%. The ECB nevertheless raised rates by 25 basis points on 10 September 2026. The deposit facility rate has been 2.50% since 16 September, with HICP inflation at 3.2% and a projection of 3.0% / 2.5% / 2.1% for 2026 to 2028. The increase serves to anchor inflation expectations and is not directed against wage pressure.

## The supply of labour

The size of the labour force is the working-age population multiplied by the participation rate. The first factor is shrinking in Germany because the baby-boomer cohorts are retiring. That leaves three levers: participation, hours per person in employment and immigration.

All three depend on legal rules. Under Section 235 SGB VI (Social Code Book VI, pension insurance), the standard retirement age is rising in stages to 67. People born in 1964 are the first cohort to whom it applies in full. If the pension starts early under Section 36 SGB VI, Section 77 SGB VI provides for a permanent reduction of 0.3% for each month brought forward, that is, 3.6% a year. Additional earnings limits for early old-age pensions have not applied since 2023 (Section 34 SGB VI). Social law therefore always affects labour supply as well.

Since October 2022, the marginal employment threshold (Geringfügigkeitsgrenze) for mini-jobs has been linked to the statutory minimum wage under Section 8(1a) SGB IV (Social Code Book IV). The formula is: threshold = minimum wage × 130 / 3, rounded up to full euros. The quotient 130/3 follows from the purpose of the rule: it means that the amount always corresponds to around 43.3 working hours a month, or about ten hours a week, whatever the level of the minimum wage.

Previously, a fixed threshold of €450 applied. Every increase in the minimum wage therefore automatically shortened the permitted working time. Here, the effect of wage policy on labour supply can be calculated unusually precisely.

First, employment and labour force participation show whether the numerator and the denominator are growing. Next, comparing wage growth with the inflation rate shows whether purchasing power is rising or falling. Finally, the rate serves as a check. If you start with the rate, the interpretation is fixed before the other figures are known.

mitnehmen: An unemployment rate can only be interpreted together with labour force participation. It can fall because people find work or because they stop looking.
Prices depend on unit labour costs, that is, wage growth minus productivity growth, rather than on the wage itself.
The real wage is the nominal wage divided by the price level. With 3.1% higher wages and 3.4% inflation, purchasing power falls by around 0.3%.
Productivity is the only source of permanently rising real wages. All other routes merely redistribute income.
The Phillips relationship exists, but it is unstable, depends on expectations and rests on a variable that cannot be observed. It is of no use for forecasts.

begriffe.text: Share of the labour force (employed plus jobseekers) in the reference population; in US statistics, the reference population is all civilians aged 16 and over who do not live in institutions, with no upper age limit. The denominator of the unemployment rate depends on it, and the unemployment rate cannot be interpreted without it.
Labour costs per unit produced. Their growth is approximately equal to wage growth minus productivity growth. For the price level, this variable matters more than the wage itself.
Value added per hour worked (or per person in employment). It is the only source of permanently rising real wages and is difficult to measure for services and digital goods.
The unemployment rate at which inflation neither rises nor falls. It cannot be observed and can only be estimated, with uncertainty bands of several percentage points.
Broader measure in German statistics that, in addition to the unemployed under Section 16 SGB III, also includes participants in labour market policy measures.
